ANOTHER SPANISH INSURRECTION.

As FRANCE has become celebrated.in_history for

_
her great revolutions, so has Spain become no-
torious for her pronuncia»lentos and paltry
insurrections. With all our sympathy for

popular movements, we really cannot designate
the Spanish attempts at revolution by any
expression conveying a serious or important
significance. We see no great principle as
cause—no large object to achieve—no compre-
hensive results to follow success, if even it
should be attained. From beginning to end,
there is an air of burlesque and unreality about
these Spanish movements. The malcontents
do not understand their own position; and if
asked what policy they are guided by, they
would be surely puzzled to give a definite
answer. So far as we have been able to trace
the many futile attempts of the Spaniards at
revolution, it would appear that they generally
arise from one cause—namely, royal favour to a
certain set of politicians, and royal neglect of all
other sets. While Espartero, O'Donnell, Nar-
vaez, or Prim flutter in the sunshine of royalty
—while their haughty and capricious mistress
condescends to smile upon them, and cover
them with her favours, no parasites of a court
could be more obsequious, or more willing to
carry out her tyrannical whims. But the
moment they are left to pine in the cold shade
of opposition their loyalty to their Queen
"oozes out at their fingers' ends," and they
proclaim themselves before the people as pat-
riots, who are ready to die sword in hand, or
even upon the scaffold if it should come to that,
in order to achieve the freedom of their country
—that is, to relieve it from bad government in
which, for the time, they have no share, and to.
substitute, if possible, equally bad government
under their own direction. We never hear of
a Spanish rising but what we grieve for the evil
that must result to the misled and ignorant par-
ticipators in it, who are sure to suffer if their
leaders do not, and without any prospect of
benefit accruing to their country. There is nei-
ther honesty enough in leading Spanish politi-
cians, nor political intelligence enough in the
people, nor sufficient patience in either, to con-
duct and control a Government upon constitu-
tional principles. On whichever side the vic-
tory may remain in a civil struggle in Spain, of
one thing we may always be assured—that no
good will come to the nation at large. The
Court of Spain is no doubt very corrupt; but
equally so are all parties of politicians, the
clergy, and the army; and, whichever party or
interest comes uppermost, it is, for the nation
at large, merely a change of men, not of things.
Nor do we see how it can be otherwise while
Spain remains socially what she now is. The
country is a perversity and a contradiction.
With a climate fruitful to excess, and with many
important natural advantages, the people court
idleness, and make no effort to advance in civili-
zation. The cities of Spain swarm with ragged
mendicants, yet the meanest of her peasants is
as haughty as a prince. Proud without any-
thing to be proud of, helpless in the hands of
an often unscrupulous clergy, and too ignorant
to recognise and seek the advantages of know-
ledge, can we wonder that the Spanish people
fail to obtain a solid benefit from any of their
numerous revolutionary movements. The pre-
sent attempt, like those which have preceded it,
is an undignified scramble of unprincipled chiefs
for power and patronage, and is sure to end in
the wholesale slaughter of their dupes who are
unfortunate enough to be drawn into the vortex.
We have no faith in the Spanish leaders. With
the exception of General Prim, they have all
been tried already; and, with their former
deeds before us, we can see nothing to hope for
from the reinstatement of any of them in the
royal favour.

THE CAFFRE WAR.

We extract the following from the Cape Frontier Thus of Aug.
4, published at Graham's-Town, from which it will be seen that
the military movements against the enemy were proceeding in a
satisfactory manner :
There are three ways of dealing with the Caffre question. A
fitter boundary than the Fish river might be chosen, beyond which
the Caffres might be driven, and the intervening space occupied
by native tribes, &c. There might be a neutral territory between
the colonial boundary and Caffreland, to be guarded against the
I approach of all intruders, black and white. Caffreland might be
brought under British control.
One or other of these measures will probably be adopted by the
Home Government. We take it for granted that it will never be
so mad or so wicked as to retain the present boundary—leaving in
independence the border tribes, a. d trusting the safety of the co-
lony to the engagements of treaties made with wild and savage
men.
It is therefore assumed that the choice of one of these plans
will be the only point for consideration. Into this choice no mo-
tive of temporary shift or expediency must be allowed to enter.
The settlement of affairs must secure not only the present, but, as
far as human foresight can determine, the future tranquillity of
the colony.
The most obvious disadvantage of the first plan is that it would
leave upon the threshold of our territory numerous bands of in-
dependent savages, who, as they increased in numbers and strength,
would become familiar with the use of fire-arms, which it would
be impossible to keep out of their hands. These armed barba-
rians would in a few years grow into a formidable enemy, to whose
depredations and open hostility the colony would again be ex-
posed.
The difficulty of maintaining the integrity of a neutral territory
is a weighty objection to the second plan. The present boundary
would still have to be guarded, and marauders pursued—besides
which the plan is open to the same serious objection as the first,—
that is, the danger of allowing the growth of armed and inde-
pendent tribes of savages on our frontiers.
The third plan seems to be the most reasonable and free from
objection. And if any opposition is made to it by the Home Go-
vernment, it will probably be from a disinclination to incur the
expense of extending the British dominions, which are considered
as being already sufficiently large and unwieldy. But if the state
of the case is properly represented at home, the Government can-
not shut its eyes to the absolute necessity of looking fully into the
troubles of the frontier, and of endeavouring permanently to put
an end to them without delay. It will find its account in acting
, thus. Any plan by which a repetition of Caffre wars can he pre-
vented must be cheaper than a system generating a Caffre war
every few years. The expense of the present war will no doubt
materially aid the Government in the development of this truth.
The inhabitants have now a great and solemn duty to perform.
They must take care that no exertions are wanting on their part
to bring about a satisfactory state of security for their persons
and property. They must see that they do not bequeath to their
children as an Inheritance the probability of suffering the horrors
of which the colony has lately been made the scene.

FRIDAY MORNING, SEPTEMBER 24, 1841

The evidence of Captain Hamilton, taken before the
Immigration Society of Trinidad, establishes the prac-
ticability of obtaining labourers from Sierra Leone for
our West India Colonies, in a manner wholly free from
objection. Mr. Hamilton was himself employed to
conduct the first attempt of this nature, and had the
good fortune to execute his commission most com-
pletely and sutcessfully. In a very short time after
arriving at Sierra Leone, he was enabled to make up
the number of emigrants he wished to obtain ; no
deceptions inducements whatever were held out to
them, and the act of their embarkation was as perfectly
voluntary as any act could be. The voyage to Trini-
dad was pleasantly performed in the short space of
thirty days, and but one human being perished on the
way—an infant under twelve months old. Captain
Hamilton remained on the island for some time after
their arrival, and visited all the estates where the
immigrants became located. He questioned them as
to the condition in which they found themselves, and
they all expressed themselves perfectly contented with
their lot. Before leaving Sierra Leone, lie pledged
himself publicly to pay the passages of six persons
back to report as to the actual state of affairs in Trini-
dad; but on applying to them, lie found that not six
persons were disposed to return, unless they were paid
Trinidad wages during their absence. We cannot
conceive any thing more conclusive as to the desirable-
ness of the move, so far as the people themselves are
concerned, than such evidence as this. There arc no
horrors in this middle passage ; it is undertaken freely.
and it is undertaken with the certainty of ameliorating
the condition of the people. The witness states, that
ten thousand persons could be immediately removed
with the greatest advantage to themselves, and to those
they would leave behind—because, in the West Indies,
they can have better wages ; and becauie, in Sierra
Leone, the labour market is over-stocked.

Ten thousand, however, being but a fraction of the
number of labourers that would be required by Trini-
dad, Guiana, and Jamaica, he is asked concerning any
other sources from which they could be procured on
the coast. To this he replies, that lie would anticipate
"a stream of immigration from the interior to Sierra
Leone, in consequence of the rise of wages that would
take place there ; so that, notwithstanding a continued
and regular emigration of labourers from thence to
the West Indies, the population of Sierra Leone would
be kept up or gradually increased."

With regard to procuring labourers from any other
part of the African coast, Captain Hamilton has some
scruples : he says, that excepting the Kroomen, few of
the natives are perfectly free and independent, and that
their removal could never be effected without first
purchasing the consent of the native chiefs." On this
point he is pressed closely, and is at length obliged to
acknowledge that his objections " partake more of
sentiment than reason." We respect such feelings,
however, as they are plainly an error, if at all such, on
the right side, and proceed from an extreme anxiety to
avoid even the appearance of evil when the abomina-
ble slave traffic dogs us at every side. The question
raised is, however, substantially this—viz., whether
one may not purchase a slave for the purpose of setting
him at liberty ? Now, we do not see any objection to
such an act. That started by Mr. Hamilton is, that
other countries would immediately claim the right to
exercise the same privilege, and use it as a cloak to
carry off the people into slavery. But we do not con-
ceive that they could claim any such privilege, unless
slavery were first entirely abolished within their terri-
tories—as it is with us.

The expense of obtaining the consent of a chief to
make his subject or vassal a free man, Mr. H. estimates
at thirty dollars, which is the ordinary price of a slave ;
the passage to Trinidad would be thirty more, so that
the whole cost of bringing over a labourer would
be but sixty dollars. Now in Brazil and Cuba the
price of a slave is estimated at 350 dollars, without
taking into account certain expenses which make the
amount really about 420 dollars. The Trinidad Com-
mittee therefore conceive that they would have a great
advantage in obtaining free labourers on terms so com-
paratively advantageous ; they conceive that with such
an advantage the planter of Cuba or Brazil could not
compete with them—and that free labour would thus
tend to drive the produce of slavery out of the market,
and to extinguish slavery itself.
The evidence is extremely interesting and important,
and cannot fail to engage attention. It leaves not a
doubt in our mind of the feasibility and perfectly un-
objectionable character of the plan of procuring free
labourers at least from Sierra Leone. Captain Hamil-
ton concludes his testimony with the following very
strong and satisfactory statement :
" It was my original intention to have remained here some
time, in order to judge of the condition and prospects of the
emigrants I brought over, and of the desirableness, or other-
wise, of recommending a further emigration. But I already
find that the people are so well off that I can be of no service
to them ; and being fully convinced of the great advantages
which the people of Sierra Leone will derive from removing
to Trinidad, it is my intention to proceed immediately to re-
commend the same in London."

Some license of speech should certainly be permit-
ted at present to our radical and dissenting contempo-
raries. They have met with very mortifying discomfi-
tures ; and there cannot be a safety valve of more ease
in the working for themselves, and of more harmless-
ness to the community, than angry and spiteful words.
Of course the clergy of the Established Church, who
have been mainly instrumental in the late victories in
Church and State, are the objects of the special hosti-
lity of " our esteemed."
A remarkable instance of this appears in the revival
by the Albion of an exploded calumny against the Rev.
Fielding Ould.

It is now nearly a twelvemonth since our contempo-
rary, stung, apparently, by the triumphant defence of
the great scriptural doctrine of the Trinity contained
in the series of sermons delivered in Mr. Ould's
church, and anxious to cover a retreat by diverting the
attention of his readers from the question -at issue to
one- of mere personalities, attacked Mr. Ould on the
charge of plagiary, and held him up to public scorn
and contempt for having attempted to pass as his own
arguments and even words derived almost verbatim
from another. We put the slanderous scribe to silence

at the time by quoting the following eaudid and manly
avowal from the preface to Mr. Ould's sermon

" It is scarcely to be expectel that, on such a subject,
much original matter should now he elicited. The praise of
originality was not, however, the author's object, but rather
usefulness and edification. Ile has accordingly availed him-
self freely of the labours of those who have gone before him
in the controversy, not only in the adoption of their argu-
ments, but frequently of their words ; and being aware how
eagerly advantage is taken of definitions and forms of ex-
pression by those whose tenets are here impugned, he has
preferred rather to clothe himself in the verbal armour of the
tried veterans in this contest, than trust himself in the weaker
panoply of his own providing."

Mr. Ould made no pretence to originality in the ser-
mon in question ; nay, he disclaims the attempt to be
original in either thought or word, plainly, boldly, em-
phatically. Having taken this course, and having thus
proclaimed-it in his preface, no reader of common can-
dour could accuse him of any affectation of author-
ship on the occasion, or any unfairness of plagiarism.

There are readers, however, and writers too, who, in
words, boast loudly their love of truth, while they ma-
nifest, practically, their hatred of candour.
Such were our contemporaries, who, after circulating
the slander, evinced too great a respect for the fairness
and good feeling of their readers, and too little a regard
for their own fairness and good feeling, to insert the
above passage from Mr. Ould's preface.
Conscious, however, of its effect in our columns,
they desisted from the base attempt to fasten upon the
reverend gentleman the charge of literary dishonesty.
Truly they must be at a loss for a subject for vitu-
peration, when they have recourse to a revival of this
charge now. The Albion has lately reiterated the ma-
lignant slander in a series of articles, in which instances
are given of Mr. Ould having done precisely what he
himself tells his readers in his preface he intended to
do. He said he would adopt the arguments of others,
and frequently their words; and because in the in-
stance of Andrew Fuller's able pamphlet, (which the
Unitarians cannot answer,) he has done what he said
he would do, the Albion and its coadjutors of the
Liberal (!) press of this town have attacked the reve-
rend gentleman as guilty of what a convenient corre-
spondent calls a " literary larceny."
Our readers will not be surprised to learn, that the
articles in the Albion which we refer to, are filled with
a vulgar levity of expression, as disgusting as the dis-
regard of truth, candour, and fair dealing, we have
now exposed, is disgraceful.
Thus, after pointing out a few instances in which
Mr. Ould adopted the language, or nearly so, of Mr.
Fuller, our contemporary says—" From the foregoing
joint-stock premises, the lean-cheeked sectary and the
smug episcopalian thus beautifully harmonise in draw-
ing a conclusion." And again—" Mr. Ould chimes
melodiously in with the defunct Dipper in the follow-
ing manner." And again—" The sharp-nosed theolo-
gical hounds thus proceed to run as a couple."
We cannot characterise such language, on such a
subject, without submitting to the defilement of imi-
tating its scurrility. We therefore content ourselves
with remarking, that it is not from attacks of this sort
our clergy need fear any loss of their well-earned re-
putation.

Mr. Ould, in opening the course of sermons to be
preached in his church, had assigned to him a branch
of the subject which had already been treated by a
master; and esteeming usefulness and edification to
his readers, rather than the reputation of originality to
himself, he availed himself of the labours of his prede-
cessors in the controversy, and openly avowed in his
preface, once for all, that he had done so. With re-
gard to Mr. Fuller's tract, we adopt gravely what the
Albion has written with an ironical sneer in the follow-
ing terms :—" In thus reviving the sentiments of this
obsolete publication, and in reviving them as they
were originally enunciated, Mr. Ould has done good
service to the religious part of the community."

He has ; and we would recommend the Albion scribe
and his coadjutors no longer to exhibit their own
weakness by evading the arguments, and their own
wickedness by assailing the individual, but at once to
grapple with the substance of Fuller's tract, as adopted
by Mr. Ould ; and if they cannot refute it, to give up
their Unitarianism, and seek admission into the Chris-
tian Church.

In the meantime we call upon them, as a matter of
common honesty, to give to their readers the passage
from Mr. Ould's preface which we have quoted above :
but we prophesy that they will be so uncommonly
honest as not to do so, because by doing so they would
at once expose themselves; and entirely vindicate Mr.
Ould from all the sneers and sarcasms by which they
have been endeavouring to injure him.

Those who suffer from thieves are naturally un-
willing to suspect members of their own household,
and require strong evidence to convince them of their
guilt. Nevertheless, it does not unfrequently happen
that much time is thrown away in seeking abroad for
the depredators—Land that when justice is near to over-
take them, the spoliated parties begin to look at home.
Something analagous to this, we fear, will be discovered
to have happened in the care of the piratical trade in
slaves, which, in spite of all that England has done to
prevent it, has been known still to go on, and, in some
unaccountable way, to flourish. Spaniards and Por-
tuguese, or their descendants, we thought, showed an
unwonted degree of energy in defeating all our labours,
and the cause seemed nearly desperate, when the dis-
covery was made, or is at least alleged to have been
made, that chief among these pirates, and busiest
amongst this flesh-dealing, thievish horde, are some of
our own energetic children—British subjects—mer-
chants, capitalists, artisans, and officers both of the
army and navy ! We can scarcely doubt the reality of
this discovery. It is very unlikely that the Committee
of the British and Foreign Anti• Slavery Society, who
profess to have made it, could be altogether deluded
on the subject; still more absurd would it be to sup-
pose that they had invented such a romance. They
have made their representation to parliament by the
hands of Lord Brougham, and they pray that its truth
may be inquired into by a committee of the house of
parliament to which his lordship belongs.
Disgraceful as are the facts to men having the pri-
vilege to be called British subjects, there is no air of
improbability on the face of the statement which would
lead us to doubt it. It is certain that there are various
mining companies in this country, with large capitals
at their disposal, who carry on their operations in
Brazil, and in Cuba, and nearly so, that, in the words
of the Society's petition, " their mines are worked by
slaves." Here, then, there is ground laid for the
charge—and the matter of inducement, as the lawyers
call it, is strong. British companies work mines in
slave-holding countries, and employ slaves themselves
on their works. What, then, suppose that they had
obtained these slaves, in the first instance, by purchase
in the country ; their first purchases, like other tools,
would wear out, and must he renewed ; or, in other
words, British subjects, by entering into such specu-
lations, have put themselves upon a level with, and in
the condition of, Brazilians and Cubans, with respect
to labour, and those morals which regard not slavery
—slavery either in its origin or its continuance—as a
crime. The next question, then, is, have the parties
subjected themselves to the penalties of the sth
George IV., which makes the act of dealing in
African slaves a transportable felony ? It seems
doubtful that they would do so, by the mere act
of purchasing slaves born in the country, or im-
ported previous to the passing of the act; but with
regard to newly-imported slaves, Lord Brougham
says that no doubt can exist that the penalty of trans-
portation for life would be incurred by such a transac-
tion. But the charge against British subjects by no
means stops at this point ; on the contrary, it goes on
till it involves them in this odious traffic in all its most
appalling forms; it casts upon them the broad impu-
tation of slave-dealing, of sending to Africa for fresh
cargoes, and of. course with all the incidents which
might be expected when that contraband and detesta-
ble traffic is unequivocally embarked in.

It is lamentable to think that there are Englishmen
capable of so disgracing their country—lamentable to
consider the number whom the one leading, guilty act
involves in its criminality. If the allegations of the
Society's petition be correct, " officers of the army
and navy, and functionaries in the civil service, have
been the agents employed in the purchase of slaves on
account of these companies"—" banks have been es-
tablished " to facilitate their operations_" goods are
manufactured in this country, in enormous quantities,
and form a considerable branch of the export trade to
Brazil and Cuba, and the western coast of Africa,

which are employed exclusively in the African slave-

" Attempt to assassinate Lord Howick !" Such,
reader, is the awful announcement which is just now
travelling in large letters through the columns of the
Whig journals. The son of Earl Grey shot at, or at-
tempted to be shot at, in the streets of the Whig-ridden
borough of Sunderland ! Awful ! Monstrous ! Hor-
rible true. Thank Heaven that we are enabled
to keep down our indignation by those two qualifying
monosyllables !

But how and when, we may be asked, was this atro-
cious crime attempted ? We must explain. At the
close of the Sunderland election his lordship, in that
amiable mood for which he is distinguished, was en-
joying, it appears, the pleasure of being borne in state
through the streets of the borough for which he had
just been returned as the representative, escorted by a
mob of colliers, lumpers, and such savoury people,
and accompanied by his lady, Sir Hedivorth William-
son, and others of his friends, when " a miscreant in
human form," whose windows the followers of the
noble lord were amusing themselves by smashing, was
observed to point a gun from an upstairs room in so
unsafe and dangerous a manner that the policeman
who saw it forthwith took to his heels, Lord Howick
himself turned very pale, and cried "A gun !" whilst
Sir lledworth Williamson, very valiantly, drew down
Lady Howick into the body of the carriage in which
they were seated together, and—fell over her !

So far, however, nothing horrific had resulted,—no-
thing beyond the serious fright of the policeman, the

" CHEAP BREAD " MEANS " CHEAP LABOUR."

There is something strongly corroborative of all which we

have ever asserted with respect to the objects of the corn-law
abolitionists, in the attempt which is now making to precipi-
tate the decision of the great question of the corn laws. If
the manufacturer looked only or mainly to the opening of
foreign markets—to the reduction of the tariffs of foreign
countries in favour of British manufactured goods—as the
result of a free trade in corn, obviously his first anxiety
would be that nezociation to effect this desirable object
should be entered upon. Markets, however, we have ever
maintained, or at least such markets as can be gained to us
by the mere concession of the power to import foreign core
into Great Britain, are not the real objects for which the
anti-corn-law league are agitating. Cheap labour it is,which
the manufacturer is in search of—cheap labour; which will
enable him to inundate every market of the world with
cheap goods—cheap labour, which will at once contribute to
raise the value of his deteriorated machinery, and which will
once more restore to him his pre-eminence over the manu-
facturers of every other nation. The attempt to compel a
settlement of the corn laws by clamour out of doors, and by
factious opposition in parliament, without at the same time
seeking, or allowing to the government of Sir Robert Peel
the opportunity of seeking, any relaxation of the continental
tariffs—any additional privileges in those foreign markets
whoie corn we are urged to purchase—is to us satisfactory
evidence of the fact, that the cry for " markets " is only
subsiding to the cry for " low wages " and " cheapness cf
production."
That this is the fact, too, may be gathered from other and
striking indications. Amidst all the diatribes of the manu-
'facturing agitators, not a word is allowed to escape which
would favour the inference that an extension of our com-
merce in foreign markets can be derived from any other
source than the adoption of a free-trade policy with respect
to articles of consumption amongst the manufacturing popu-
lation. Market after market has been closed upon our mer-
chants, by the blundering and inefficient policy of whip le-
gislators ; yet we hear not a word of complaint against the
policy which has thus crippled our commerce. Our goods
are virtually excluded from at least half-a-dozen important
foreign countries—from Spain and Portugal—from a large
portion of the coast of Africa—from China and other mar-
kets ; yet we hear not a word of any sincere desire to seek
for readmission, into these. We hear of nothing, in fact,
but the markets of the corn-growing countries ; and these
even are put forward, not as being in themselves of any
overwhelming value to the manufacturing interest, but as a
cloak to the real object in view, which is " low wages to the
manufacturing population."

We admit all that is urged by the advocates of a prompt
settlement of the corn question, with respect to the wretched
condition of the manufacturing population and their misera-
ble prospects during the approaching winter. We know that
agitation will spare no exertion to render that condition in-
supportable, and to goad the suffering poor into frenzied
excesses. But we cannot by any means admit that the ex-
istence of such misery, or the contemplation of its too pro-
bable results, should impel any statesman to rush upon a
hasty and undigested settlement of the corn-laws or any
other laws. What legislation in conservative hands can do,
in the judicious exercise of its power to give an impulse to
commerce, the government of Sir Robert Peel will do.
But, upon the corn-law-repealer's own shewing, that impulse
can only be given, through the medium of a free trade in
corn, by the aid of negociation with the governments of fo-
reign countries. By the mere repeal of the corn laws we
derive no relaxation in the tariffs of foreign states ; and we
should therefore, by hasty measures, be only throwing out
of our hands the power of compelling a return for the sacri-
fice which we are called upon to make.
Conservatism is manifestly not in fault that nothing is
done in the present session to relieve the embarrassments
into which whig mismanagement has thrown every great in-
terest throughout the country. Whether whig adhesion to
office, for four months after their power to legislate for the
community had ceased, is blameable, we leave to the com-
munity itself to declare. Lord John Russell can see in
September the importance of adopting measures for the re-
lief of the labouring classes, immediately. Pity that his
lordship was blind to this pressing necessity during the four
months which intervened between the rejection of his budget
in April, and the day on which he reluctantly bid adieu to
Downing-street and the Horne-office !

A CONTRACT is a mutual promise. The obligation, therefore, of contracts; the sense in which they are to be interpreted; and the cases where they are not binding, will be the same as of promises.

From the principle established in the last Chapter, "that the obligation of promises is to be measured by the expectation, which the promiser any how voluntarily and knowingly excites," results a rule, which governs the construction of all contracts, and is capable, from its simplicity, of being applied with great ease and certainty, viz. That,

Whatever is expected by one side, and known to be so expected by the other, is to be deemed a part or condition of the contract.

CHAPTER VII.

CONTRACTS OF SALE.

THE rule of justice, which wants most to be inculcated in the making of bargains, is, that the seller is bound in conscience to disclose the faults of what he offers for sale. Amongst other methods of proving this, one may be the following:

I suppose it will be allowed, that to advance a direct falsehood in recommendation of our wares, by ascribing to them some quality which we know that they have not, is dishonest. Now compare with this the designed concealment of some fault, which we know that they have. The motives and the effects of actions are the only points of comparison, in which their moral quality can differ; but the motives in these two cases are the same, viz. to procure a higher price than we expect otherwise to obtain; the effect, that is, the prejudice to the buyer, is also the same; for he finds himself equally out of pocket by his bar gain, whether the commodity, when he gets home with it, turn out worse than he had supposed, by the want of some quality which he expected, or the discovery of some fault which he did not expect. If therefore actions be the same, as to all moral purposes, which proceed from the same motives, and produce the same effects; it is making a distinction without a difference, to esteem it a cheat to magnify beyond the truth the virtues of what we sell, but none to conceal its faults.

It adds to the value of this kind of honesty, that the faults of many things are of a nature not to be known by any, but by the persons who have used them so that the buyer has no security from imposition, but in the ingenuousness and integrity of the seller.

There is one exception, however, to this rule, namely, where the silence of the seller implies some

Contracts of Sale.

111 fault in the thing to be sold, and where the buyer has a compensation in the price for the risk which he runs as where a horse, in a London repository, is sold by public auction, without warranty; the want of warranty is notice of some unsoundness, and produces a proportionable abatement in the price.

To this of concealing the faults of what we want to put off, may be referred the practice of passing bad money. This practice we sometimes hear defended by a vulgar excuse, that we have taken the money for good, and must therefore get rid of it. Which excuse is much the same, as if one, who had been robbed upon the highway, should allege he had a right to reimburse himself out of the pocket of the first traveller he met; the justice of which reasoning the traveller possibly may not comprehend.

Where there exists no monopoly or combination, the market price is always a fair price; because it will always be proportionable to the use and scarcity of the article. Hence, there need be no scruple about demanding or taking the market price; and all those expressions, "provisions are extravagantly dear," "corn bears an unreasonable price," and the like, import no unfairness or unreasonableness in the seller.

If your tailor or your draper charge, or even ask of you more for a suit of clothes, than the market price, you complain that you are imposed upon; you pronounce the tradesman who makes such a charge dishonest: although, as the man's goods were his own, and he had a right to prescribe the terms, upon which he would consent to part with them, it may be questioned what dishonesty there can be in the case, or wherein the imposition consists. Whoever opens a shop, or in any manner exposes goods to public sale, virtually engages to deal with his customers at a market price; because it is upon the faith and opinion of such an engagement,

Contracts of Sale.

that any one comes within his shop doors, or offers to treat with him. This is expected by the buyer; is known to be so expected by the seller; which is enough, according to the rule delivered above, to make it a part of the contract between them, though not a syllable be said about it. The breach of this implied contract constitutes the fraud inquired after.

Hence, if you disclaim any such engagement, you may set what value you please upon your property.

If, upon being asked to sell a house, you answer that the house suits your fancy or conveniency, and that you will not turn yourself out of it under such a price; the price fixed may be double of what the house cost, or would fetch at public sale, without any imputation of injustice or extortion upon you.

If the thing sold be damaged, or perish, between the sale and the delivery, ought the buyer to bear the loss, or the seller? This will depend upon the particular construction of the contract. If the seller, either expressly, or by implication, or by custom, engage to deliver the goods; as if I buy a set of china, and the china-man ask me whether he shall bring or send them to me, and they be broken in the conveyance; the seller must abide by the loss. If the thing sold remain with the seller, at the instance, or for the conveniency of the buyer, then the buyer undertakes the risk; as if I buy a horse, and mention, that I will send for it on such a day, which is in effect desiring that it may continue with the seller till I do send for it; then whatever misfortune befals the horse in the mean time, must be at my cost.

And here, once for all, I would observe, that innumerable questions of this sort are determined solely by custom; not that custom possesses any proper authority to alter or ascertain the nature of right and wrong; but because the contracting parties are presumed to include in their stipulation, all the conditions which custom has annexed to contracts of the same sort; and when the usage is notorious, and no

Sermons alone did not suffice the evangelicals. It was their great business to make a solemn confession of their faith before the Diet. One day, which it is not easy to determine, but probably about the end of July, 1530, Tausen and his friends appeared before the king, the grandees of the realm, the bishops, and the deputies, and presented, respectfully but boldly, the statement of their faith. Their declaration did not possess the perfect form of Melanchthon's confession, with which they were at present unacquainted; but it had more clearness and force. While Luther's friend, from a wish to spare and even to gain over the powerful princes who listened to him, had passed over in silence certain articles which might have given rise to sharp contradiction, Tausen and his brethren did not think it their duty, in the presence of haughty and persecuting bishops, either to soften the statement of their doctrines, or to spare the Romish party.

HEN in any department of science we find certain laws established
and almost universally admitted, and that the most celebrated men
in the branch in question not only give credence to these laws, but constantly
bring forward facts to support them and bear them out, we are not a little
surprised to find some one who asserts that these laws are unfounded. In the
little book which Mr. Hopkins has just issued, we are somewhat astounded to
find that hitherto we have been travelling in darkness. Our knowledge has
been faulty and full of error, and our mode of framing inductions has been
unsound. Mr. Hopkins, however, in the true spirit of philanthropy, has
determined to enlighten us. No longer shall we stray from the paths of truth,
with the guiding light of his genius to point out the way. It is, indeed, a
melancholy reflection, that in this, the second half of the nineteenth century,
we have made such a slight advance toward a knowledge of the Statute-book
of Nature. Is it not humiliating to find such men as Lyell, Ramsay,
Murchison, and Logan existing in a very mire of ignorance? Yet that such is
the case Mr. Hopkins has assured himself. What Galileo did for Mechanics,
Harvey for Physiology, and Newton for Astronomy, Mr. Hopkins bids
fair to achieve for the future of Geology. The author of the volume before us
returns to his native land, after a minute survey of the universe, including,
of course, the less-distant planet, and, for the benefit of humanity, he
expounds the comprehensive generalizations which his genius has unfolded.
He does not do so from any desire of distinction. Friends who will read
former essays occasionally press hard upon an author, and compel him, nolens
volens, to appear again in the arena of literature. So did it fare with
Mr. Hopkins. Anxious, after a lifetime spent in the investigation of natural
phenomena, to retire, like another Cincinnatus, from the field of his fame,
he was driven by friendly pressure to appear again before the public.

part of the world, solely for the love of scientific truths, he feels pleasure in

not had the opportunity of studying the world as it is," and "in order to
show that the actual operations of terrestrial physics and geological changes
do not warrant the extravagant speculations now entertained by geologists."

The feelings awakened by the scenery of the
forest, are unlike any others. You sit down in a
moonlight_evening, after a day of hard fatigue,
and look off. You are on a fine knoll some
twenty-five feet higher than the lake before you.
That lake is now as calm, and as still, and as
bright as if molten silver. Its sarface is only
broken, here and there, by the large trout or sal
mon, as he throws out his fluked tail. The is
lands covered with forests, loom up in the mirage,
and seem to move and float and all seems like a
fairy land. The lofty mountains rise up all a
round, and seem to stand in the majesty of soli
'tude. They repose like monsters, too independent
to emit a single sound. Their sides are covered
with the richest trees, whose leaves are dyed, in
the pure atmosphere of autumn, orange, straw,
yellow, crimson, scarlet, and carmine.-They
look as if a thousand rainbows had fallen to piec
es and dropped their glories upon them. Not a
sound is heard save the distant seream of the
lonely loon, or it may be the howl of the wolf, or
the peculiar who-ha-ho of the laughing owl."
The fishing eagle has uttered his last scream for
to-day, and the blue heron has taken his mis
shapen form 1o the tall pine for the night. Your
camp-fire sends-its light far up among the magnif
icent trees around you, and makes them look
like so many mighty pillars sustaining a canopy
of silver; while beyond the reach of your light,
the forest seems a thousand times darker than
common darkness. At the head or the foot of the
lake is the heavy waterfall, now sending up its
hoarse roar usa part of nature's evening hymn.
Perhaps, too, as was the case with us on one oc
casion, your tent is pitched close by a tree which
hias a large cross cut deep into its wood. Your
guide tells you what it means. It is the monu
ment of some Indian who lies buried in front of
that cross. How far off we know not. 'T'he In
dians would know, and go at ouce to the spot.
But you only know that a son of the forest lies
'buried close by, and the solitary grave near you
contains one who will start up at the call of the
archangel's trumpet. What griels, or joys, or
deeds were his, will not he known until that day.
These graves are scattered through the wilder
ness, and the memorial will long remain, for the
hunter is very far from being the man to cut down
these trees. I hardly need add that they are
probably the graves of the St. Francois Indians,
who are Catholics, and who know little more a
bout religion than to mark the cross as the sign of
salvation When you are thus in the midst of a
great forest, knowing that you must go fifty or
sixty miles ere you can reach a human beingknowing that here man has left no prints of his
puny foot-that God himself reigns here in soli
tude, you have a subdued feeling of dependence
and insignificance that is new and peculiar. You
feel that you might fall like one of the leaves
that is filfling around you, and the forest would
stand, the mountains cast their deep shadows,
and the lake mirror back the bright heaveus,
and the world move on just as if you bad never
been.

Should the bore of the tube be uneven or
irregular curvatures, or should the parts on
each side of the zero-point not be symmet-
rical, the ends of the bubble, as they aug-
ment or diminish in length by changes of
temperature, would not rest exactly equi-
distant from the zero-point, or mark equal
divisions on the scales. The tangent, how-
ever, to the zero-point would be horizontal,
although the bubble would have an apparent
inclination; and therefore, to bring the ends
of the bubble to coincide with the equi-dist-
ant divisions of the scales, would be to give
the tangent an inclination, and throw the
instrument out of adjustment. This results
more or less with all unground or defective
tubes, and consequently sections plotted, es-
timates made of work, and works set out and
regulated from levels taken or given by such
tubes, must be in error in proportion to
their imperfection.
In levels of precision, especially those
employed for astronomical and engineering
purposes, the interior surfaces are made
truly even and cylindrical, and with a sens-
ible curvature upwards exactly to an are of
a circle, by grinding them with emery-pow-
der and oil or water on steel cylinders, and
then polishing them. This process is re-
peated until the bubbles prove, by turning
the tubes end for end on a delicately-ad-
justed support, to be perfectly symmetrical,
or until the ends appear at, or mark pre-
cisely equal distances from the middle or
zero-point, the tangent to which is then hor-
izontal.
Hence, in the preparation of these tubes
the chief objects to be attained are, uniform-
ity of bore, perfection of curvature, and
smoothness of surface; and it should be ob-
served, in conclusion, that whatever care
and finish are bestowed on the exterior
mountings of the tube, if the interior of the
tube itself be imperfect in the above res-
pects, the tangent given by the bubble will
not be horizontal. Tubes have been and
can be made to indicate a point half a sec-
ond of a degree from exact horizontality, or
within one-hundredth of a foot of horizon-
tality at the distance of one mile. This
slight deviation is due, not to the principle
of the instrument, but to mechanical defects,
from which no instrument, however deli-
eately made, is absolutely free.

The culture of Flax is becoming a very important
branch of agricultural pursuit. But a few years since,
if a farmer sowed more than a bushel of flax-seed, un-
less he was a very extensive farmer, he was considered
by his neighbors as bordering on insanity. The great
majority of farmers in those days, sowed but a few quarts
of seed, with the view more particularly of raising flax
rather than seed. It is now no uncommon thing for
farmers to sow twenty, thirty and sometimes fifty bus els
and upwards; and notwithstanding the flax is usually
destroyed, the seed alone, as a general thing, pays as
well and frequently better, than any other crop. The
flax is considered of no value from the fact, that the
expense of pulling, rotting, dressing and preparing for
market, over balances its worth, and hence farmers have
resorted to the most expeditious modes of getting rid
of it, such as burning it, throwing it into wet marshy
places, &c. I have recently had conversations with
several farmers, who have for the last two years engaged
quite largely in raising it, who assure me that if the
flax is cut before it becomes "dead ripe," by paying
the same attention to it in curing it that is usually be-
stowed upon the securing of hay, cattle will not only
eat it readily, but are very fond of it, besides it keeps
them in a very thriving, healthy condition. Those
persons with whom I conversed, agreed in their belief,
that the flax thus secured, is worth almost, if not quite,
as much as the seed,
I wish to mention another impertant fact in relation
to raising flax-seed, which every farmer should know.
Several farmers of my acquaintance, the past season, sowed
flax-seed and barley on the same ground, and in every
instance the yield of either kind, was as great as if
sowed separately, besides flax and barley straw com-
bined, makes very excellent fodder. By having proper
screens, there is no difficulty in separating the flax-seed
'from the barley. If, by sowing flax-seed and barley
| together, twice the amount can be obtained from the
| Same ground, is it not worth at least the consideration
of every farmer? N.

ence to the practice of growing flax and barley together,

| would be matured while the stalk was in so green a
| State as to be good for fodder; but it will be seen that

and that at the same time a crop of seed is obtained in

FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN ENGINE

DRIVER.

On Saturday a melancholy accident occurred at Hez-
ham-station on the Newcastle and Carlisle section of the
North-Eastern Railway to an engine driver named
Edward Atkinson. It appears that deceased was the
driver of a train which was proceeding to Carlisle, and
stopped at lierham for the purpose of taking in water.
Whilst the engine was under the water tank deceased
commenced to oil the machinery, and was so engaged
when the train from Carlisle came in eight. Deceased
observing the train approaching was in the act of stepping
on to his engine, but missing his footing he was struck
by the buffer of the advancing engine and knocked on
to the rails, and the whole of the train passed over him.
The poor fellow, when picked up, was found to have
sustained severe injuiies, but was still alive. Medical
aid was at once procured, but he died in a few hours.

SECTION III.

PARAGRAPHS.

1. The Importance of Paragraphs.

A PARAGRAPH is a group of sentences that are closely related in thought. The great importance of paragraphs is evident from the definition. They serve to give distinctness to the sequence of thoughts.

Probably the usual neglect of paragraphing is owing to an imaginary difficulty in the art. A few simple rules will serve to make the subject plain.

Nearly all the works on composition almost ignore the division of discourse into paragraphs, and, as a consequence, many otherwise good writers either make no paragraphs or place every important sentence by itself.

2. Rules for Paragraphs. (1) Make an analysis before writing. This may be either written or mental, according to the character and extent of the composition.

This direction is of very great importance, and after a few trials its great advantage will be evident. In a short time the habit of making a mental analysis will be formed, and every composition will gain in clearness, because of the methodical arrangement of the thoughts.

(2) Make each distinct point in the analysis the subject of a paragraph. All the sentences written to expand, explain, or illustrate this germ thought will have a connection that will justify their being grouped together.

A paragraph is made by commencing on a new line, a short distance from the beginning of the line. The sentences are then written in close succession, until the paragraph is completed. This group of sentences is a paragraph. (3) Observe unity in the construction of a paragraph. This rule excludes all digressions from the principal thought of the paragraph. No sentence has any right to a position in connection with others, unless it is closely related to the preceding or the following sentence.

It is frequently advisable to state the main thought in a brief and clear sentence. This may be placed at the commencement of the paragraph, and then explained, illustrated, proved, or contradicted, as the case may require; or, it may be placed at the end, as a kind of summary or conclusion. (4) Construct the sentences so as to secure variety in their length and rhythm. Monotony results from a continued uniformity of length or structure. No one kind of sentence is absolutely the best. Here, as everywhere in composition, variety is an excellence.

The first sentence of a paragraph should be as short as the sense will permit. It is discouraging to a reader to find himself lost in a labyrinth at the very beginning. When interest and feeling have been aroused, longer sentences are more appropriate. A very short sentence after a very long one is objectionable.

Variety in a paragraph may be of less importance than some

STYLE.

73 other quality. For example, if a paragraph be devoted to a continued antithesis, a uniformly balanced structure of sentences should be studied, as in the celebrated parallel betweer

Homer and Virgil. "Homer was the greater genius; Virgil the better artist; in the one, we most admire the man; in the other, the work. Homer hurries us with a commanding impetuosity; Virgil leads us with an attractive majesty; flomer scatters with a generous profusion: Virgil bestows with a careful magnificence. Homer, like the Nile, pours out his riches with a sudden overflow; Virgil, like a river in its banks, with a constant stream."

A style characterized chiefly by short sentences is called by the French the style coupé. When the sentences are long, and closely joined by conjunctions, we have the style periodique.

The first is adapted to familiar, light, and informal writing · the latter, to elaborate, exact, and dignified composition. (5) Make the paragraph progressive in meaning and in sound. There is little reason for writing unless thought grows with the marshalling of words. As in a sentence, so in a paragraph the effect should be cumulative. Hence the last sentence should seldom be a short one, but more sonorous than its predecessors. A terse and forcible summary of a paragraph constitutes a fitting close, but it must be full of meaning or it will seem insignificant.

This rule forbids " writing in a circle," which is almost as grave a fault as "reasoning in a circle;" and the two vices are often companions. A writer who holds this rule in mind will never become tedious to an intelligent reader He will bring his paragraph to a close when he has once expressed his thought, and not strain after the unattainable through endless repetitions (6) Connect the sentences so that their relations will be obvious. This is of vital importance. The highest art is required to cause the stream of thought 1

to flow smoothly, bearing the reader along without doubts or interruptions. Sentences are connected by the co-ordinate conjunctions, and the expression of continuous thought, accordingly, requires skill in their management.

The importance of using proper connectives is illustrated under the third rule for Compound and Complex Sentences. A few additional observations may be of value in this connection.

Subordinate conjunctions connect clauses; co-ordinate conjunctions connect sentences. The co-ordinate connectives are:

3. Illative; as, {therefore, wherefore, hence, consequent- It is by the proper use of these connectives that isolated threads of thought are woven into a beautiful fabric. It requires as much judgment, however, to avoid the excessive use of conjunctions as to use them correctly. CHAPTER XI.

ACROSS WHALE SOUND.

THE storm broke at about midnight, but the sky remained overcast during the following day. We turned out early in the morning, and looked around us to ascertain our position. Everything was wintry. Deep snow-drifts lay along the shore and under the hill. Our tent was nearly buried. Above us rose a dark cliff, on the south of which was a steep declivity, from which the snow had all been. blown into the deep valley on the margin of which we were encamped. The ice had been driven in by the gale, and was pressed tightly against the shore.

The coast of the mainland, terminating in Cape Parry, lay on the left, and Northumberland Island on the right. We had drifted far up Whale Sound, and now occupied Herbert Island, at least such was our conjecture.

There appearing no prospect of our being able to put to sea, I took a gun and, accompanied by Godfrey, set off up the valley in search of game.

After a toilsome journey through the deep snow, we reached the table-land which forms the culminat-

ing ridge of the island. There our views respecting our position were confirmed. The ice-pack filled up the channel and extended far to the southwest.

BURGOMASTER-GULLS.

115 We reached the camp late in the afternoon; having seen, but not captured, a fox, and having discovered the footmarks of a hare. Petersen had had better fortune. He was sleeping soundly in the tent, after dinner, when he was aroused by one of the men calling to him that a flock of "burgomasters " were floating in a pool a little way up the beach.

Running hastily out, without stopping to dress, he killed and secured nine out of eleven. The materials for two good meals were thus added to our commissariat. What we most needed, was fuel.

There remained only a few pounds of the fat which had been brought from the ship for such use. This we were saving for an emergency; and during the last few days we had been burning pork, confidently expecting to capture a seal or a walrus, and thus to secure a good stock of blubber; but hitherto we had been uniformly disappointed. Several of these animals had been observed, but they were so shy that we could not approach them. The foxes had exhibited the same timidity. Many of these, as already stated, had been discovered on Northumberland Island, and I was puzzled to explain the cause of their shyness. Petersen declared that a little fellow whom he wounded soon after landing, had told his comrades of the murderous character of our guns, and that thus forewarned, they kept clear of us! At all events, be the cause what it might, they sustained the reputation of their race for cunning. The readiness of the seals to take alarm I could more easily understand, for a relentless war is waged against them by the natives. They are often wounded, and escape from their pursuers; while the foxes, taken only in

traps, never live to tell tales. The product of our guns, thus far, had been eighteen burgomaster-gulls, twelve eider ducks, seven foxes, and one raven, in all, about forty-eight pounds. We had obtained, besides, from the hut at Anoatok, eight pounds of walrus meat, half of which remained to us; but the great question now was, how should we procure material for fire? If necessary, we could eat, uncooked, such food as we might have; but how, without fire, should we obtain water? for, henceforth, we must mainly depend upon melting the snow or ice. In the afternoon Mr. Sonntag was fortunate enough to find a little rivulet, from which the kettle was filled.

This enabled us in the evening to obtain a cup of coffee, which luxury the scarcity of our fuel would otherwise have compelled us to deny ourselves. The day was calm, for the most part; but as the sun went down, the wind blew again from the southwest. Temperature, 2610.

I was too much fatigued to make the circuit of the island; and I am, therefore, not able to add anything to the chart of Captain Inglefield, who, in the little steamer Isabella, ran up the channel in August 1852. The cliffs above us were composed of sandstone and slate, resting on primitive rock, which was visible near our camp. About a quarter of a mile above us were discovered two well built Esquimau huts, which appeared to have been recently occupied.

Hoping that fortune would continue to favor our effort, we retired again to our tent, and awoke on the following morning to find that the wind had hauled around to the northeast, and that the clouds

"HUK! HUK! HUK!" 117 were breaking away. By one o'clock, P. M., it was quite clear. The thermometer went up to two degrees above the freezing point; the ice was giving way, and long leads were opening through it, in every direction. A narrow belt of heavy floes joined together by young ice, unfortunately lay close along the shore; otherwise we could have launched our boats at two o'clock. To break through this belt would have occupied us until night; and deeming it imprudent again to trust ourselves in the darkness to an uncertain channel we concluded to remain where we were, and to start fresh with the early morn.

The morn broke upon us bright, clear, calm, and summer-like. The young ice, neither strong enough to bear nor frail enough to yield easily, seemed for a time likely to baffle us; but by breaking it up with our boat-hooks and poles, we finally succeeded in effecting our escape; not, however, until an hour after the sun had passed the meridian. The way appeared to be free toward the mainland, for which we pulled. After we had been under oars a couple of hours, a light breeze sprang up from east-northeast; once more our canvas was spread, and our ears were again gladdened by the music of gurgling waters as the boats rushed onward through the rippled sea.

We struck the coast at about twenty miles above Cape Parry. Passing under the north cape of Burden Bay, we were surprised to hear human voices on the shore. That they were Esquimaux we knew from the peculiar "Huk! Huk! Huk!"-their hailing cry. Upon approaching the land, a man and a

boy were discovered running down the hill toward the beach; and when we came near they were standing close to the water's edge. Petersen held a conversation with the man, w the boy ran off over the rocks and was soon out of sight.

The man was "Kalutunah," the Angekok* of his tribe, and one of our friends of last winter. He informed us that he lived at a short distance up the bay, where there was a colony of his people, to which he invited us to accompany him; promising that we should have some blubber and meat, and that he would pilot us into the harbor if we would take him into our "Oomeak." The boy had gone to spread the alarm; and, while we were parleying with Kalutunah, a crowd of men, women, and children, with a great number of howling dogs, were seen streaming toward us along the shore, all running at full speed, flinging their arms about, and mingling their voices together in unintelligible gleefulness. The chief burden of their exclamations seemed to be "Kabulenet! Kabulenet! Oomeak! Oomeak!" "White men and ships! white men and ships!" To avoid the impetuous avalanche, we drew hastily alongside of a rock, and, taking the Angekok on board, pushed off and pulled toward the settlement, the crowd following us along the beach. The prospect of getting some blubber justified us in losing a little time.

Our pilot had never been in a boat before; and he seemed to experience all the enjoyment of a child at the possession of a new toy. "Tek-kona! tek-kona! 99 "Look at me! look at me!" was his

The bay was covered with pancake-ice,* which greatly retarded our progress; and it was nightfall when we reached the settlement, a mile and a half up the bay. The whole colony eagerly assisted us in landing the boats and in carrying up the cargo.

About twenty of them, as if it were fine sport, seized the painter and the gunwale, and endeavored to imitate us in every motion; breaking out into loud peals of laughter whenever they made a mistake. The subject which caused them most merriment was the "Heave-oh!" of the sailors. This they attempted to imitate; and it was very amusing to observe their efforts to chime in and keep time.

They could not approach nearer than "I-e-u ! "

They afterward i-e-u-d everything, and "I-e-u! i-e-u!" rang through the settlement the livelong night.

We were landed in a little cove. To the right and left, about thirty yards apart, stood two masses of rock twenty feet high, which nicely protected our harbor. The summits of these little capes were level; and on the table to the right we pitched our camp and stowed our cargo. of the convict establishment at Fremantle gives his views
upon convict discipline, of which he ought-to know some-
thing, as follows :—" Sooner or later the industrial
employment of prisoners will be abandoned in all
civilised countries, and for it will be substituted a sys-

strictest solitary confinement, from the day of reception

and symbol of freedom and integrity, and idleness as
both the effective cause and scourge of crime."

-• The outrage which was committed in New Hereford-
street on Monday morning takes us back to a period offour
years 'ago, when the murder in Acorn-street, and
outrages upon person and property in various parts of
the town had cast a stigma upon the name of Sheffield,
from which it has never fairly recovered. The far-famed
attempt to blow up Wastnedge's house, in Acorn-street;
the horrible mutilation of Mrs. Wastnedge, and the
death of her poor old lodger, Mrs. Bourke, created a
feeling of abhorrence so intense that for a time outrages
-of that-kind seemed to have become things of the past.
The disclosures made on the trial of Thompson for that
murder deepened the painful feeling with which Sheffield
was regarded in the distant towns o• • and this feeling
seemed to have reacted upon the people at home,: for the
leaders of the trades' unions vied with each other in de-
nunciation of these outrages and the motives which led
to their Perpetration. It seems, however, that the.dernon
has not yet been exorcised, and the latest manifestation
of its presence might have been the most barbarous and
, shocking in its consequences of the whole series.
It seems that the man Fearneyhough is a saw grinder,
in the employment of Messrs. Butcher aad Co., and up
to 12 months ago he was a member of the Saw
Grinders' Union. Circumstances took place which in-
duced him to leave the union, and since that time, with
the exception of one occasion, he has shown a determi-
nation to go on his own way. He states that several
months ago some negotiations took place with the view
of his readmission into the society-, but that the sum
which was demanded (£l3) as the price was too large,
and he broke off the treaty. Since that time he has
lived in apprehension that an attempt would be made to
injure him, and, unhappily, he could refer to too . many
previous outrages upon saw grinders to justify his
fears. On Sunday night he went to bed with his
family at the usual hour, having first carefully
fastened the -small iron grate over the entrance to
the cellar. In the house there were seven persons
sleeping, and in the house behind, which is built "back
to back" with it, were seven other persons. Abdtt half-
past 5 o'clock, according to the concurrent testimony of
a number of persons, a loud report was heard, 're-
sembling the discharge of a small cannon, and. in an
instant Feaxneyhough and his family were awakened
and found their house in ruins. The man rushed down-
.stairs and into the street at once, but he could see
nobody about. He then turned back and assisted his
family down the crumbling stairs into the street, which
by this time was half filled with the tenor-stricken in-
habitants of the adjoining houses. The explanation of
the scene that met their gaze was not for a moment
doubtful. All the symptoms, so to speak, of a " trade out-
rage" were there, and an examination of the premises
confirmed the truth of the conclusion. In the cellar the
fragments of an "infernal machine" were found. It
would seem that the grate had been forced open, and a
metal can, tightly wrapped with cord to increase
the force of the explosion, and containing about
two pounds of gunpowder, had been thrown into
the cellar. It was exploded in the usual manner
by a fuse, which was probably long enough to en-
able the assassins to fly from the neighbourhood before
the -explosion took place. The force of the explosion
was very great, and in all probability, if the house had
been of stronger construction, it would have blown up
the bed-rooms, and thereby caused the death of the in-
mates. As it was, the blast seems to have rushed up
the cellar staircase, blown the door into fragments, and
then spent its force on the side of the house and stair-
cases leading to the bedrooms. The destruction is so
,complete that the escape of the inmates of the house
seems marvellous. The windows and the shutters of
the living room were blown out and across the street.
The house is next to an entry, and the dividing wall is
only one brick in thickness. Fortunately, this
gave way at once, and the force of the ex-
plosion spent itself in the passage in a great
,degree. Enough was done, however, in the house,
to show how great the danger had been. The stair-
oases and the supporting walls had been split from top
to bottom; the windows and doors were shattered to
pieces, and the whole of the house-side seemed to be
on the point of falling in a mass. The house behind,
occupied by a family of seven persons, named Jepson,
was also seriously damaged, but very fortunately, out
of the 14 persons who were thus exposed to the hazard
.a frightful death, not one was injured. This remark-
able result reminds us of a similar outrage in Bramber-
street some years ago, when a house was partly blown
to pieces by an infernal machine without any of the
inmates being injured.
The explosion was heard at a considerable distance,
and crowd of persons flocked to the scene at once.
Great sympathy was manifested for Fearneyhough and
his family, and the utmost horror and detestation of the
perpetrators of the crime. The Chief-constable visited
the scene at an early hour, and took possession of the
fragments of the exploded can.

The present generation is certainly not fortunate
in being fated to witness so many distressing events,
and to behold so many nations and races afflicted
with the scourge of war, and the cruel calamity of
despotic tyranny. Mr. COBDEN was certainly very
nzal apropos some years ago in his prophesy of a
general peace pervading the world. Instead of
that blessed advent there seems general war and
universal discord. The last startling announcement
that reaches us concerns the Caucasians, and pain-
ful to the feelings as have been the several items of
intelligence that have been forwarded to us from
time to time concerning the state of the nations
that are the theatres of war, it would seem as if
this last event bids fair to rival, if not surpass, the
other casualties. It is always a distressing and
disastrous occurrence when a brave race has to
give way at last, and a gallant band of patriots falls
before the ruthless attacks of merciless and unscru-
pulous invaders. The Russians, with that perse-
verance that always accompanies their warlike
efforts, and that savageness that unfortunately
distinguishes their natures, have pursued their
course of conquest, and kept firm to their work of
extermination. Such a picture as is presented to
our view of the sad state and bitter miseries of this
helpless and persecuted people seems almost incre-
dible to realise by civilised states, and repugnant
to the very nature of all humane people. What
evils must have been endured, what cruelties in-
flicted, and what an appalling prospect for the future
presented itself to their view harrows the thoughts
to contemplate and fills the imagination with
horror. Really when we read of these transactions
we may ask, Where is the vaunted progress of the
age ?—has it made peace an easier possession ?—has
it deserted war and its horrors ?—has it oven kept
alive the chivalric feeling that in the earlier days
of the world's history made honourable some of the
most deadly strifes, and softened the harsh outlines
of attacks and invasion ? Nowadays it would
seem as if to spare the vanquished, to moderate the
rigour of conquest, and to apply the golden rule
that is applicable in war as in peace were quite
uuthought of. At all events, Russia has set a stern
example to the less powerful nations, and, judging
from recent accounts, Prussia has not been slow to
follow in her wake, nor slack in her endeavours to
compete for the gains won in the unworthy manner
described. It will long be remembered as a lasting
disgrace to the Prussians that their persecutions
nhould have compelled their unfortunate victims to
resort to the adoption of this unnecessary expedient,
and to expose themselves, their women and children,
to the perils, fatigues, and miseries of this unpre-
pared for and unparalleled expedition. It. is difficult
to decide in what particular phase of their fearful

undertaking the outcasts of this noble race suffer
the most, or are the most to be pitied. Whether
waiting on the shore for the means of transport, or
in the act of crossing the Euxine in the crowded
and miserable vessels, or again when landed at their
destination, in all the horrors of over-stocked places
and contagious diseases, it is impossible to say
which is the worst. The details of their adventures r '
in the several stages are most harrowing to dwell
upon, and must make the reader shudder to
contemplate. To think a:so that these decimating
inflictions and excruciating torments have been
endowed by a noble race, adds tenfold to the
horrors of the reflection, and renders it difficult to
restrain one's indignation in due bounds. It is
difficult for those who arc accustomed to the incon-
sistent and equable rule of constitutional govern-
ment to csmprehend the motives of those who thus
constantly urge on an exterminating war, and per-
sists
in the face of all remonstrances from other
nations to follow out their preconceived policy.
The only solution that can be found is in the want
of humanising feeling that is so lamentably deficient
in the Russian, as also in some other states.
This want is, indeed, most painfully in the details
of the Circassian exodus. Seldom has it fallen to
the lot of the present generation to peruse such a
harassing recital as that which is here presented
before us, and it naturally suggests itself to the
mind to consider the circumstances that have led to
the sad casualty, and the consequences that may
ensue from its occurrence. There can be no doubt
that it is the tyranny of the Russians that has led
to their departure. That rule has been of such 6
class that it involves resistance even from the con-
quered, and causes men to undertake the must des-
perate measures rather than abide undt r its sway.
The best proof of the invincible character of their
determination is that those who still remain are re-
solved to follow, notwithstanding the fearful priva-
tions and sufferings to which their predecessors have
been exposed. It is truly observed in the account of
this sad affair that the " sacrifice of independence
alone would surely not have induced 300,000 people
in a body from their country." Also, they
to fly
would have adopted more prudent and precautionary
measures before proceeding on such a momentous
expedition. It is quite idle for the Russians to say
that they have endeavoured to take steps to con-
ciliate the people. No one of any discernment can
possibly attach credence to such an assertion. The
stern denial to their declaration is given in charac-
ters that none can fail to mark. The brave but
unfortunate Circassians have rendered a solemn
protest against the cruelty of their barbarous op-
pressors in the sight of GOD and Man, and the
nations must look on with awe at such a fearful
visitation befalling a noble race, and with indig•
nation at the barbarity that propels the deed. It
is to be trusted that in the land of their adoption
these unhappy exiles may meet with a better fate,
but that will not condone the conduct of those who
have driven them forth from their hearths and
altars, from the graves of their fathers and the soil
of their birth.
